strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem: the paper is the first to address decoding arbitrary, text-specific information-seeking goals (rather than procedural reading-task categories) from eye movements, filling a genuine gap between psycholinguistic work on goal-driven reading and cognitive state decoding in NLP.

The task design is thoughtful: the two-tier evaluation (different vs. same critical span) probes decoding at different levels of semantic granularity, and the critical-span annotations provide a principled way to make the task progressively harder.

Comprehensive and careful experimental methodology: 10-fold cross-validation with disjoint New Participant / New Text / New Text & Participant regimes, article-level splits, proper statistical testing via linear mixed effects models with random intercepts and slopes, and 95% confidence intervals.

Strong set of models: simple interpretable RT-similarity baselines, adapted state-of-the-art discriminative models (Haller RNN, RoBERTEye-Fixations), and two new generative multimodal LLMs (DalEye-LLaVA with a novel eye-movement encoder, DalEye-Llama with textual fixation representations), evaluated on both selection and open-ended reconstruction.

The reconstruction evaluation is unusually thorough for an open-ended decoding task: question word, UIUC category (validated against human annotators, kappa 0.794), BLEU, BERTScore, and a creative downstream QA-accuracy metric, benchmarked against meaningful baselines including human-composed distractor questions and text-only decoding models.

Good reproducibility: public dataset, detailed hyperparameter search spaces, prompts, and model specifications in the appendix; explicit ethical considerations covering consent and potential misuse of gaze decoding.
weaknesses: Absolute performance is modest: the best model achieves 49.3% three-way selection (57.3% same-span) and reconstruction quality largely degrades to near-baseline levels in the New Text regime, so the practical significance of the results is limited; the paper's framing ('considerable success') slightly overstates what is shown.

The task setting is somewhat constrained and artificial: each paragraph has only three candidate questions, readers are explicitly given the question before reading, and questions are relatively short (mean 10 words) over short paragraphs (mean 109 words). Generalization to genuinely open-ended, naturalistic information seeking remains untested, so the 'open-ended' claim should be qualified.

The generative models are at a structural disadvantage in the selection comparison (not trained on the selection objective), which complicates the discriminative-vs-generative comparison; a generative model fine-tuned for selection, or a matched training objective, would make the comparison cleaner.

Limited analysis of what the models actually learn: no error analysis, attention/interpretability analysis, or linguistic analysis of which goal types are decodable; the scientific insight promised in the introduction (nature of the relation between task conditioning and reading behavior) is not deeply explored.
The New Text & Participant regime uses only ~1% of test trials, making those numbers noisy; the paper could better acknowledge this asymmetry.

Some evaluation choices are debatable: the QA-accuracy metric depends on a fixed RoBERTa QA model and only the 86% of questions it can answer, and BLEU/BERTScore comparisons against same-span human questions are confounded by lexical overlap, as the authors themselves note.

strengths: Genuinely novel task formulation: the paper moves beyond 'procedural' reading-goal classification (e.g., ordinary reading vs. annotation in prior work) to 'semantic', text-specific goal decoding, which is a new challenge for cognitive-state decoding from eye movements.

Well-designed task structure: the critical-span design (two questions sharing a span vs. one with a distinct span) enables two difficulty tiers, and the paper is commendably transparent about the non-obvious chance accuracies (33.3%, 55.5%, 50%) including the 'Monty Hall' subtlety.

Comprehensive and rigorous experimental protocol: 10-fold cross-validation with three generalization regimes (new participant, new text, both), proper mixed-effects statistical testing accounting for non-i.i.d. structure, and extensive appendix documentation of architectures, features, hyperparameters, and prompts.

Both discriminative baselines (Haller RNN, RoBERTEye-Fixations) and two new generative multimodal LLMs (DalEye-LLaVA with a novel eye-movement encoder, DalEye-Llama with a textual fixation representation) are developed and systematically compared, including ablations over prompts and eye-movement representations.

Thoughtful evaluation of free-form reconstruction: five complementary metrics (question word kappa, UIUC category kappa, BLEU, BERTScore, downstream QA accuracy) benchmarked against meaningful reference baselines (incorrect human questions, GPT-4o/Llama arbitrary questions, text-only decoding model), with human agreement validation of the GPT-4o categorizer.
Good ethical considerations section (privacy/biometric concerns of eye tracking, risks of unreliable assistive applications) and a reproducibility statement; dataset is public.
weaknesses: The 'arbitrary, open-ended goals' framing is somewhat stronger than the evidence: goals come from a closed set of only 3 human-authored questions per paragraph (486 total), so the task is still a constrained selection/generation problem rather than truly open-ended goal decoding.

Absolute performance is modest: best three-way selection accuracy is 49.3% (RoBERTEye-Fixations), and only 57.3% on the same-span tier; reconstruction in the hardest (new text) regimes is weak (question-word kappa ~0.07, QA accuracy at or below the human same-span baseline), so the practical claims (real-time educational/assistive applications) are distant from current results.

Generative models underperform the discriminative ones on selection, and DalEye-LLaVA is at chance across most settings; the contribution of the newly proposed multimodal architectures relative to adapted prior encoders is limited, and the reconstruction analysis covers only DalEye-Llama.

Reconstruction evaluation relies on heuristic proxies; no human judgment study of generated questions, and the QA-accuracy metric depends on a RoBERTa/RACE model whose answerable subset (86%) introduces selection effects.

Scope limitations: single dataset (OneStop), English only, native adult readers only, ~10-word questions and short paragraphs; generalization beyond this setup is untested, and the model-selection procedure across unknown evaluation regimes introduces some ambiguity.

The main text is largely descriptive of results; there is limited analysis of what eye-movement signals drive success (e.g., which features or reading behaviors are informative), which would strengthen the scientific contribution.

strengths: Novel and clearly motivated task: this is, to my knowledge, the first work to decode arbitrary, text-specific information-seeking goals from eye movements, going beyond prior procedural goal-decoding work (Hollenstein et al., 2021b; Shubi et al., 2025) that distinguished a small set of text-independent reading manners. The procedural vs. semantic distinction is well articulated in the related work section.

Well-designed two-tier task formulation (goal selection across different critical spans vs. the harder same-critical-span setting), with the critical-span design cleverly supporting graded difficulty and informative chance baselines (including the Monty Hall subtlety in the Different Spans regime, correctly noted as 55%).

Comprehensive modeling comparison: simple embedding-similarity baselines, two adapted state-of-the-art discriminative eye-tracking models (Haller RNN, RoBERTEye-Fixations), and two new generative multimodal LLMs (DalEye-LLaVA, DalEye-Llama), covering both discriminative selection and open-ended reconstruction.

Rigorous evaluation: 10-fold cross-validation, three generalization regimes (new participant / new text / both), balanced question-type distribution, hyperparameter search per split, and statistical testing via linear mixed effects models with random intercepts and slopes for participants and paragraphs, correctly handling the non-i.i.d. structure.

Thoughtful reconstruction evaluation: five complementary metrics (question word Kappa, UIUC category Kappa with validated GPT-4o annotation at 0.794 kappa, BLEU, BERTScore, and a novel downstream QA-accuracy criterion), benchmarked against strong and well-analyzed baselines including human distractor questions whose span-sharing effects are carefully interpreted.

Generous appendix with full model details, prompts, eye-movement feature tables, and complete result breakdowns; ethics and reproducibility sections are present and address biometric identification risks and consent explicitly.
weaknesses: Absolute performance is modest and results are heavily concentrated in the easier regime: the best model reaches only 49.3% on three-way selection and, critically, the advantage in the Same Span regime is small (57.3% vs. ~50% chance). The open-ended reconstruction claim is weakened by the sharp drop in the New Text regime, where DalEye-Llama falls behind the human-distractor baselines on BLEU/BERTScore/QA accuracy; the paper is somewhat guarded but the abstract's 'progress towards free-form reconstruction' rests mainly on the New Participant regime where the text was seen in training.

Evaluation relies on a single dataset (OneStop), a single language, and a constrained task space (three candidate questions per paragraph, each tied to one of two critical spans). Claims about 'arbitrary' goals are therefore bounded; generalization of the task definition and models beyond this benchmark remains untested.

Generative models underperform the discriminative ones on selection and DalEye-LLaVA is essentially at chance, so half of the newly proposed modeling contribution yields largely negative results; the analysis of why (e.g., frozen backbone, LoRA capacity, representation choice) is limited to input-variant ablations without deeper diagnosis.

Reconstruction metrics are heuristic; the downstream QA-accuracy criterion depends on a RACE-fine-tuned RoBERTa's idiosyncratic behavior (restricted to the 86% of questions it answers correctly), which may not track human-equivalent goal recovery, and no human judgment study of reconstruction quality is provided.

Prior work by an overlapping author group (Shubi et al., 2025, 'Decoding reading goals from eye movements', ACL) already addresses goal decoding on the same dataset; while the semantic/text-specific framing is new, the delta over this closest prior work should be quantified more explicitly (e.g., a head-to-head baseline), and code release is not explicitly committed in the reproducibility statement.
No analysis of what eye-movement signals drive success (e.g., attention to critical spans), which would strengthen the scientific claims about goal-driven reading that motivate the paper.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated task: decoding text-specific, semantic reading goals (rather than procedural reading modes) from eye movements is a genuinely new challenge that meaningfully extends prior work (Shubi et al., 2025; Hollenstein et al., 2021b), and the procedural-vs-semantic distinction is clearly articulated.

Comprehensive model suite: the paper compares simple interpretable baselines (RT-weighted embedding similarity), strong adapted discriminative models (Haller RNN, RoBERTEye-Fixations), fine-tuned generative LLMs (DalEye-Llama, DalEye-GPT, DalEye-LLaVA), and frontier LLM prompting (Gemini zero-/few-shot), giving a full picture of the modeling landscape.

Rigorous evaluation design: 10-fold cross-validation with three disjoint generalization regimes (New Participant, New Text, New Text & Participant), article-level split partitioning to avoid leakage, linear mixed-effects models with random slopes for statistical testing, and careful handling of the Monty Hall-type chance structure (Appendix E).

Thoughtful baselines for the generative task: human incorrect questions (same/different critical span), text-only fine-tuned LLMs, and arbitrary LLM questions cleanly isolate the contribution of eye movements above textual priors and potential pretraining contamination — a concern the authors explicitly address.

Valuable cognitive analysis: the mixed-effects analysis linking model performance to interpretable gaze features (e.g., reading time within vs. outside the critical span) ties the ML results back to psycholinguistic theory and positions the model as an analytic tool for information-seeking research.
Reproducibility: public dataset, released code and all generated outputs, detailed hyperparameter search, prompts, and training procedures in the appendix.

Thorough ablations (feature groups, input representations, prompt variants) and extensive appendix results, including honest reporting of the underperforming DalEye-LLaVA and weak generalization to new texts.
weaknesses: The 'open-ended' framing is somewhat overclaimed: each paragraph has only three candidate goals, and the selection task is a 3-way classification over a closed candidate set (or binary variants). Truly open-ended goal decoding over an unconstrained hypothesis space is only partially approached via the reconstruction task, where results are modest.

Absolute performance is moderate: best 3-way accuracy is 49.3% (vs. 33% chance), and Same Span discrimination is only 57.3% (vs. 50%). In the New Text regime, generative models' advantages over text-only baselines shrink or disappear on some measures, so the practical significance for the envisioned applications (education, assistive tech) remains distant.

The goal reconstruction evaluation relies on heuristic surface/semantic measures (BLEU, BERTScore, GPT-4o-based category labels, a RACE-finetuned RoBERTa QA proxy); only the category labeling is validated against human judgment (86% agreement, one author annotator), and no human evaluation of reconstruction quality is reported.

Discriminative models are adaptations of existing architectures (Haller RNN, RoBERTEye) rather than new methods; the generative contribution is largely prompt/representation engineering around off-the-shelf LLMs.

Scope limitations: single language (English), a single controlled dataset collected with a lab-grade EyeLink tracker, and only 162 paragraphs / 486 questions, raising questions about generalization to real-world web reading scenarios the discussion motivates.

The scientific claim that eye movements alone carry goal information is entangled with the discriminative model's access to the text; the feature ablations show substantial redundancy and that linguistic features alone achieve much of the Different Spans performance, tempering the strength of the eye-movement-specific conclusion in that regime.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated task: decoding arbitrary, text-specific information-seeking goals from eye movements is a genuinely new challenge that goes beyond prior procedural goal classification (Hollenstein et al. 2021b; Shubi et al. 2025), and the paper positions this procedural-vs-semantic distinction clearly.

Comprehensive evaluation design: the split of test data into New Participant, New Text, and New Text & Participant regimes properly handles the non-i.i.d. structure of eye-tracking data, and the two-tier difficulty (different vs. same critical span) is a thoughtful analysis of what the signal actually reflects.

Statistically rigorous: linear mixed-effects models with random slopes/intercepts for participants and paragraphs, explicit chance-level derivations (including the Monty Hall subtlety in Appendix E), and Bonferroni-corrected coefficient analysis are well above the norm for this area.

Strong and fair baselines: the text-only and human-composed question baselines cleverly isolate the contribution of eye movement information, including controlling for possible pretraining contamination of OneStopQA text — a concern the authors proactively address.

The cognitive linking analysis (Figure 4) tying model success to goal-directed reading behavior (longer dwell in critical span, shorter dwell elsewhere) adds genuine scientific interpretability beyond raw benchmarks.

Good coverage of model families (discriminative encoders, finetuned generative LLMs, frontier zero/few-shot LLMs), feature ablations, and alternative eye-movement representations; code and data release support reproducibility, and ethical considerations are thoughtfully discussed.
weaknesses: The 'open-ended' claim is overstated: with only three candidate questions per paragraph, the goal selection task is a small closed set, and the generative reconstruction is evaluated mostly against questions the models have effectively seen the distribution of. True open-ended goal spaces (arbitrary user goals) remain untested, so the framing in the title and abstract is stronger than the evidence.

Absolute performance is modest: RoBERTEye-Fixations reaches 49.3% three-way accuracy (chance 33%) and only 57.3% on the same-span binary task (chance 50%). The headline results are above chance but far from practically deployable, which tempers the significance of the applications sketched in Section 8.

Limited model novelty: all core models are adaptations of existing architectures (Haller RNN, RoBERTEye, LLaMA/GPT-4o finetuning, LLaVA-OneVision). The contribution is primarily the task, dataset usage, and analysis rather than methodological innovation.

Reconstruction evaluation is heuristic and somewhat noisy: question-word and GPT-4o-based UIUC category accuracy are coarse; BLEU/BERTScore are confounded (the incorrect human baseline with the same critical span wins on both), and the downstream QA-accuracy metric depends on a RACE-finetuned RoBERTa that itself fails on 14% of the questions.

Weak generative generalization to new texts: performance drops substantially in the New Text regime and DalEye-Llama often fails to beat its text-only counterpart there, which undercuts the claim that eye movements add robust value in the harder, more interesting setting.

Single dataset, single language, lab-grade eye tracker (EyeLink 1000 Plus), and highly controlled stimuli (Guardian paragraphs, 3 questions each) limit external validity for the real-world applications (web browsing, e-learning) proposed in the discussion.

Some details reduce clarity: the New Text & Participant regime is only 1% of test trials, making conclusions there statistically fragile, and the mixed use of intercepts-only vs. random-slope models across different analyses is not fully justified.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated task formulation: moving from 'procedural' goal decoding (small fixed category sets) to 'semantic', text-specific goal decoding, including a challenging free-form goal reconstruction variant. This is a genuinely new challenge in cognitive state decoding from eye movements.

Extensive and careful experimental design: 10-fold cross-validation with three generalization regimes (New Participant, New Text, New Text & Participant), balanced splits, article-level split assignment, and Monty Hall chance-accuracy analysis for the different evaluation tiers.

Statistically rigorous evaluation: linear mixed-effects models with random intercepts/slopes for participants and paragraphs account for the non-i.i.d. data structure; Bonferroni correction in the cognitive analysis; appropriate significance marking throughout.

Strong baseline design for the generative task: human-written incorrect questions, text-only finetuned variants, and arbitrary LLM questions effectively isolate the contribution of eye movement information, including mitigating concerns about pretraining contamination with OneStopQA.

Meaningful cognitive analysis: linking model performance to interpretable gaze features (e.g., reading time before/within/after the critical span) provides converging scientific evidence and positions the model as an analytical tool, not just an engineering artifact.
Comprehensive appendices: hyperparameter search spaces, feature lists, prompts, ablations, numerical results with statistical tests, and released code/model outputs support reproducibility.
Honest reporting: the paper candidly reports weak generalization to new texts for generative models, at-chance results for heuristic baselines, and the underperformance of DalEye-LLaVA.
weaknesses: Limited modeling novelty: the discriminative models are adaptations of existing systems (Haller RNN, RoBERTEye-Fixations) and the generative models are largely prompt-based finetunes of off-the-shelf LLMs (Llama, GPT-4o-mini, Gemini). The core contribution is the task and evaluation framework rather than technical innovation in modeling.

Restricted scope: a single dataset (OneStop Information Seeking), single language (English), native adult readers, three candidate questions per paragraph, and relatively short paragraphs (~109 words). Generalization claims about 'arbitrary, open-ended goals' rest on a fairly narrow goal space (486 questions, 3 per text), which is far from truly open-ended.

Absolute performance is modest: 49.3% on three-way selection (chance 33%) and 57.3% on Same Span (chance 50%). While statistically solid, the practical significance of the decoding is limited, and the paper's forward-looking application claims (assistive technologies, real-time personalization) outpace what the evidence supports.

Generative reconstruction degrades substantially in the New Text regime, and the text-only Llama 3.1 baseline is the strongest baseline in the New Participant regime across all five measures, raising questions about how much of the eye-movement benefit is realized; results also vary by evaluation metric with no single consistent winner.

Evaluation of generated questions relies on heuristic proxies (BLEU, BERTScore, question word/category accuracy, downstream QA accuracy); a human evaluation of semantic equivalence of reconstructions is missing, which limits the interpretation of 'meaningful progress' in the reconstruction task.

Some reliance on proprietary models (GPT-4o-mini finetuning, Gemini-3-Preview) hinders full reproducibility of those components, and the GPT-4o-based UIUC categorization, while validated (0.794 kappa), injects LLM-based measurement into the evaluation pipeline.
The feature ablation shows small effect sizes and substantial redundancy across feature groups, leaving the mechanism by which eye movements contribute only partially characterized.
